topic.title: Diwali has one film
topic.claim: At Diwali the family picks one film and every other release loses, because a festival ticket is a group decision and not a taste decision.
topic.behaviour: Families book seats together and choose what everyone, including the grandmother, can sit through. The weekend chart was lopsided: Ramayana took ₹174.00 crore of the top five's ₹252.75 crore net, and Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.
topic.mechanism: Theatres give shows to whatever fills the hall, and groups fill the hall for the film that is safe for all ages. A hit gets more screens, which makes it look even bigger.
topic.group: People who go to the movies with family at festival time
topic.moment: You wanted to see a different film this Diwali, but the family plan had one name on it.

turn.believed: The biggest film wins because it is the best film.
turn.actually: It wins because a group of different ages can agree on it, and screens then follow the crowd.

topic.feeling: Part of a crowd and slightly left out of your own choice
topic.villain: A screen-allocation system that rewards whatever fills the hall in the first weekend
topic.because: Exhibitors earn from full halls, so they move shows to the film families choose. The second-choice film loses its place even if people liked it.

proof.fact: Sacnilk puts the top five films at ₹252.75 crore net for the Diwali weekend, with Ramayana taking ₹174.00 Cr (69% of that). Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because they lost screens.

topic.payoff: A festival hit is the film the whole family could say yes to, not necessarily the one anyone loved most.
topic.send_to: The friend who always ends up watching what the family picks
real_details: Scene grew on both Saturday and Sunday, unlike the usual front-loaded star release
topic.news_peg: Sacnilk's Diwali weekend (November 6-8) box office report (2026-11-09)
topic.why_now: The Diwali weekend numbers have just come out.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: The first premise: that Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because theatres took away their screens, not because of audience preference. Both films were losing their audiences before Ramayana opened. Jailer 2 came out on 15 Oct 2026, so Diwali weekend was its fourth weekend. Its India net fell from about ₹311 Cr in week 1 to ₹105 Cr, then ₹42 Cr. Its active screens dropped from a peak of 3,279 on 22 Oct to 977 by 5 Nov and 377 by 6 Nov, before the Diwali weekend. The collections fell first and the screens followed. In Tamil Nadu its main Diwali competition was three new Tamil releases, not Ramayana. AK 47 earned ₹12.75 Cr on its day 3 and ₹3.75 Cr on day 4, a Monday drop of about 70% that also came before Ramayana arrived. Pinkvilla does name Ramayana as a major reason for AK 47's later fall, but it also says the film 'didn't record a good hold in the earlier few days.' Losing screens was a result of weak demand, not the main cause of the slide. The idea that theatres fill shows by expected occupancy is broadly right. I could not verify the 69%-of-top-five figure.. How it actually works: Indian multiplexes split ticket revenue with distributors and revise show allocations every week, mostly based on advance bookings and how full the previous week's shows were. A film's screen count tracks its audience: screens are withdrawn after collections drop. In a festival week, a new event film with heavy advance bookings, such as Ramayana with about ₹50 Cr in advance sales, takes over the shows that ageing or fading films had already lost demand for. Jailer 2 was in week 4 and had already shed most of its screens, and AK 47 had already slumped on its first Monday. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.
Could not confirm: 'Jailer 2 and AK 47 were among the top five films this Diwali weekend and their earnings slipped.' (the cited pages don't say it). Use a source that does, or cut it.
Could not verify: 'Ramayana is the film the families chose as the one everyone in the row could agree on.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.

7f35c7d6a869cd8799d6e2c1f54799ba142c1460.broken_premise: The first premise: that Jailer 2 and AK 47 slipped mainly because theatres took away their screens, not because of audience preference. Both films were losing their audiences before Ramayana opened. Jailer 2 came out on 15 Oct 2026, so Diwali weekend was its fourth weekend. Its India net fell from about ₹311 Cr in week 1 to ₹105 Cr, then ₹42 Cr. Its active screens dropped from a peak of 3,279 on 22 Oct to 977 by 5 Nov and 377 by 6 Nov, before the Diwali weekend. The collections fell first and the screens followed. In Tamil Nadu its main Diwali competition was three new Tamil releases, not Ramayana. AK 47 earned ₹12.75 Cr on its day 3 and ₹3.75 Cr on day 4, a Monday drop of about 70% that also came before Ramayana arrived. Pinkvilla does name Ramayana as a major reason for AK 47's later fall, but it also says the film 'didn't record a good hold in the earlier few days.' Losing screens was a result of weak demand, not the main cause of the slide. The idea that theatres fill shows by expected occupancy is broadly right. I could not verify the 69%-of-top-five figure.
7f35c7d6a869cd8799d6e2c1f54799ba142c1460.actual_mechanism: Indian multiplexes split ticket revenue with distributors and revise show allocations every week, mostly based on advance bookings and how full the previous week's shows were. A film's screen count tracks its audience: screens are withdrawn after collections drop. In a festival week, a new event film with heavy advance bookings, such as Ramayana with about ₹50 Cr in advance sales, takes over the shows that ageing or fading films had already lost demand for. Jailer 2 was in week 4 and had already shed most of its screens, and AK 47 had already slumped on its first Monday.
